title: Mars Rover
statement:
NASA lands rovers on a rectangular plateau. The plateau is a grid from (0, 0) (bottom-left) to (X, Y). A rover has a position and a heading: N, E, S or W.

Commands: L and R turn 90° left or right on the spot. M moves one cell forward. North is y + 1, east is x + 1.

Write def solution(spec). spec is the text input: the first line is X Y, then two lines per rover: its start x y H and its command string. Rovers move one after another. Return each rover's final x y H, one per line, joined with \n.

In this first version, rovers never leave the plateau.

examples.why: The original kata input. Rover 1 loops a square and moves up one; rover 2 zig-zags to the east edge.
Up two, turn right to face east, across two.
An empty command line: the rover stays where it landed.

constraints: each command string has 0..100,000 characters from L, R, M
lines may have stray spaces or blank lines between them

think.q: What state does one rover have, and what changes it?
think.a: Three things: x, y, heading. L/R change only the heading; M changes only the position, in the direction of the heading.
L: N turns to W. M: west means x - 1. Result 0 2 W.

think.q: What's the first thing you'd write?
think.a: A big if/elif for every heading and every command (16 branches). It works but is easy to get wrong and hard to extend when the interviewer adds a command.

"commands", "one after another", "final position" → simulation. The trick is to make turning data, not code: keep 'NESW' in clockwise order, so R is index + 1 and L is index - 1, both mod 4. A dict maps each heading to its (dx, dy).

1. Split into non-blank, stripped lines.
  2. For every pair of lines after the first: parse x y H, then loop over the commands.
  3. L/R: rotate with the index trick. M: add STEP[H].
  4. Collect f'{x} {y} {H}'; join with \n.
Empty command line. A rover with no command line at all (last line missing). Four turns in a row (back to the start heading). Extra spaces and blank lines. A 0 x 0 plateau.

hints: Keep the headings in clockwise order: DIRS = 'NESW'. Turning right is DIRS[(i + 1) % 4], turning left is DIRS[(i - 1) % 4].
Parse with [ln.strip() for ln in spec.strip().split('\n') if ln.strip()] and walk the rover lines two at a time: range(1, len(lines), 2).
explain:
The whole kata is one loop per rover. The only clever bit is turning: with headings in clockwise order N E S W, a right turn is the next letter and a left turn the previous one, wrapping with % 4. Moving is a table lookup of (dx, dy).

  • 1 2 N + L → W, M → 0 2, L → S, M → 0 1, L → E, M → 1 1, L → N, M M → 1 3 N.

In a pair-programming round, say this out loud, write a test for the classic input first, then make turning data-driven so the next extension is a one-line change.
complexity: O(total commands) time, O(rovers) extra space for the output

govtech.evidence: Glassdoor GovTech Software Engineer reviews (2026) list "Roving on Mars hacker rank" next to "Design a chain of consensus system"; another 2026 SWE report says Mars Rover came up in the video-call round after the HackerRank test.
extensions: A move that would leave the plateau, or hit another rover or a rock, must stop the rover: see Mars Rover II.
Make the planet round: driving off one edge brings you back on the opposite edge: see Mars Rover III.
Add a B (move backward) command. With the data-driven STEP table this is x -= dx.
Refactor into a Rover class with turn_left(), turn_right(), move(), and a Plateau that answers is_free(x, y). Interviewers watch whether new rules land in one place.
Validate input: reject unknown commands or headings with a clear error instead of crashing.
